page: Google Cloud Platform e2-standard-2 is a general-purpose virtual machine instance belonging to the E2 machine family. It is configured with 2 dedicated vCPUs, mapped from 1 physical Intel Xeon core with hyper-threading enabled. The instance features 8.0 GB of system memory, providing a balanced 4.0 GB of RAM per vCPU. The underlying CPU operates at a base frequency of 2.2 GHz and includes a 55 MB L3 cache. It supports x86_64 architecture with hardware-assisted virtualization, Advanced Vector Extensions (AVX), and AES cryptography. This instance does not include local NVMe SSD storage or bundled GPUs, and it does not provide complimentary public IPv4 addresses.

Benchmark evaluations place the e2-standard-2 in the lower tiers of compute and memory performance. In stress-ng testing, the instance achieved a single-core CPU score of 1103.39 and a multi-core score of 1451.58, indicating limited processing capacity for parallel workloads. Memory bandwidth tests show 79.92 GB/sec for cached small-block reads, dropping to 11.77 GB/sec for large-block uncached reads and 10.27 GB/sec for large-block writes. Geekbench 5 testing yielded a single-core score of 867.0 and a multi-core score of 1025.0, with similar low-tier performance observed in software compilation, ray tracing, and image processing. Database operations, measured via Passmark, scored 826.31, while Redis SET operations reached 1.35 million operations per second.

Given its hardware profile and benchmark results, the e2-standard-2 represents a cost-efficient option for workloads with modest resource requirements. The trade-off for its lower pricing tier is reduced performance density and limited throughput, as evidenced by a static web serving throughput of 1.45 GB/sec and an LLM inference speed of 64.91 tokens per second for text generation on a small 135M model. This instance is best suited for lightweight applications, small-scale web serving, development and testing environments, basic background tasks, and low-traffic database operations where high-performance compute and memory bandwidth are not critical.
